competitors.name: Crimson Education
competitors.what: Premium, high-touch admissions consulting (US/UK/Ivy+ focus) bundled with tutoring, test prep, extracurricular mentoring and an online high school (Crimson Global Academy).
competitors.model: B2C high-ticket service packages sold by sales/strategy teams; upsells tutoring and online schooling. Founder-led brand (Jamie Beaton) and admissions-results marketing.
competitors.pricing: Not publicly listed. Wikipedia reports programmes from upwards of USD 25,000, with some families paying close to USD 200,000; older TechCrunch figure: USD 5-10k average revenue per US student, tutoring from USD 80/hr.
competitors.scale: Series D of NZ$67m led by Movac (announced 5 Nov 2024) at a valuation above NZ$1bn; FY2024 revenue exceeded US$100m; 22 offices on five continents; Crimson Global Academy ~1,700 enrolments from 60+ countries. (CB Insights gives a lower USD 640m valuation figure, so sources conflict.)
competitors.why_it_works: Sells to aspirational, affluent families where the outcome (top-university admission) is extremely high value; heavy outcomes marketing; vertical bundle (counselling + tutoring + school) raises lifetime value per family.
competitors.take: The bundle logic: one student relationship that spans test prep, tutoring, essays and applications. Publish verified outcome stats. Offer a premium human-counselling tier (Navigator+) for families who want it.
competitors.difference: Meridian is priced for Georgian incomes (29-79 GEL/mo vs. five-figure USD packages), Georgian-language, and covers non-Ivy pathways (UWC, FLEX, Erasmus+, free European tuition, summer schools) that Crimson underweights.

competitors.name: CollegeVine
competitors.what: US college-admissions platform for students: free chancing engine, school lists, essay peer review, and a free AI counsellor (formerly 'Ivy', renamed 'Sage'). Since May 2024 it also sells AI recruiter/advisor agents to universities.
competitors.model: Freemium for students (free core tools; paid essay reviews and paid human advising) plus B2B SaaS to universities (AI Recruiter, AI Advisor, AI Ambassador).
competitors.pricing: Third-party reviews cite premium essay reviews at USD 19.99/mo or USD 199/yr and paid advising around USD 1,300 (unverified on CollegeVine's own site).
competitors.scale: About USD 31m raised per CB Insights, including a USD 24m Series B (April 2019). AI Recruiter adopted by 50 institutions within two months of its May 2024 launch (company press release). A third-party review claims Sage has served 81,000+ students.
competitors.why_it_works: Free data-driven tools (chancing) built a large student audience cheaply; that audience and data became leverage to sell to universities. The pivot shows student-paid counselling alone was hard to scale.
competitors.take: Free 'chancing'/fit tools as a top-of-funnel hook; two-sided model where institutions pay to reach the student audience Meridian builds.
competitors.difference: CollegeVine is US-only and US-data-trained; reviews say its chancing skews optimistic at selective schools. Meridian can calibrate guidance on Georgian/Qatari applicant realities (financial aid for internationals, national exam context) and cover non-US destinations.

competitors.name: Leverage Edu
competitors.what: Indian study-abroad platform: counselling, application/admission support, plus financing (Fly: loans, forex) and accommodation.
competitors.model: Revenue mainly from student placement services (over 90% of FY24 operating revenue), i.e. university-side placement fees, plus commissions on loans, forex and accommodation.
competitors.pricing: Counselling pricing to students could not be verified from public sources.
competitors.scale: Revenue from operations Rs 173 crore in FY25 (up 91% from Rs 90.6 crore in FY24) with a reported Rs 106 crore loss (Entrackr, from RoC filings). Series C of USD 40m (2023, led by ETS) at a reported ~USD 150m valuation.
competitors.why_it_works: Huge volume market (India outbound students) where universities pay recruitment commissions, letting the platform offer cheap/free counselling and cross-sell finance. Still loss-making, showing high CAC.
competitors.take: Ancillary revenue around the student journey (loans, housing, forex, visa) once students have offers; university partnership revenue.
competitors.difference: Commission-driven agents have a conflict of interest (steer students to paying universities). Meridian can position as independent/student-first and transparent about any partner listings.

competitors.name: Leap Scholar (Leap)
competitors.what: Indian full-stack study-abroad company: free counselling, IELTS prep, university discovery, plus student loans via Leap Finance.
competitors.model: Students pay nothing for counselling; partner universities pay Leap a commission only after successful enrolment. Paid IELTS prep and lending as extra revenue lines.
competitors.pricing: Counselling free to students (company FAQ); IELTS course prices not verified.
competitors.scale: USD 65m Series E (Jan 2025) led by Apis Partners; Inc42 lists ~USD 318m total funding including a USD 100m HSBC debt facility (2025). FY24 revenue reported at Rs 175-203 crore depending on Inc42 page (inconsistent).
competitors.why_it_works: Combines a high-volume, low-cost funnel (IELTS prep, content, community) with university-paid commissions and lending, so counselling is subsidised. Transparent FAQ on how it earns from universities builds trust.
competitors.take: Use test prep (IELTS/SAT) as the acquisition engine that feeds counselling; disclose clearly how Meridian earns money from partners.
competitors.difference: Leap is India-only and commission-based; Meridian is Georgia/Qatar-first, bilingual, and includes non-degree opportunities (exchange, summer, youth, startup programmes) that agents do not monetise.

competitors.name: LEAF (American-Georgian Education Center)
competitors.what: Tbilisi-based study-abroad centre (since 2008) offering college counselling, SAT/TOEFL/IELTS prep, and a twice-yearly international education fair in Tbilisi.
competitors.model: Fee-based counselling and test-prep courses; event/fair model connecting students with universities.
competitors.pricing: An archived LEAF page listed 450 GEL per university or 1,500 GEL for a package of up to 5 universities, with 10-15% discounts on SAT/TOEFL/IELTS courses (date unknown; may be outdated).
competitors.scale: Self-reported: helping students since 2008, 'thousands' studied abroad; site counters show placeholder zeros, so scale is unverified. Next fair listed 29 March 2026, Tbilisi.
competitors.why_it_works: Long local track record, physical presence and fairs build trust with Georgian parents; Georgian-language content on studying in USA/Germany/EU ranks in search.
competitors.take: Run (or partner on) physical events/fairs; publish Georgian-language guides per destination country; per-university pricing is a simple local benchmark.
competitors.difference: LEAF is a traditional service agency with limited product/tech; Meridian offers a searchable programme database + globe, AI assistance, a tutor marketplace and subscription pricing well below a 1,500 GEL package.

competitors.name: Tbilisi study-abroad agencies (IEC, ELL, Your Education, GAA, Anglo-Georgia Global Group, AdAstra)
competitors.what: Traditional agencies offering university selection, admission paperwork, entrance-test registration and visa help. Several (e.g. IEC, AdAstra) mainly recruit international students INTO Georgian universities rather than sending Georgians abroad.
competitors.model: Typically commission from foreign/partner universities plus student service fees; specifics not published.
competitors.pricing: Not published; directories such as UniAgents state they do not charge students, but agency fees vary and are unverified.
competitors.scale: Listed on UniAgents/education agent directories (e.g. ELL established 2001, Anglo-Georgia Global Group 2008). No verifiable user numbers.
competitors.why_it_works: Face-to-face trust and visa/paperwork handling; university commissions make basic help cheap for families.
competitors.take: Visa and document-checklist support is a real pain point worth adding as content or a paid add-on.
competitors.difference: Fragmented, opaque pricing and commission conflicts; little digital product. Meridian can be the transparent, verified, digital-first option.

competitors.name: EducationUSA - Center for International Education, Tbilisi
competitors.what: The only comprehensive EducationUSA advising centre in Georgia, part of the U.S. State Department's EducationUSA network, advising on study in the US.
competitors.model: Government/grant-funded advising (U.S. Mission to Georgia also runs EducationUSA grants of USD 25-50k for organisations).
competitors.pricing: Fees could not be verified (EducationUSA advising is generally free or low-cost, but not confirmed for this centre).
competitors.scale: Official EducationUSA centre listing; no student numbers found.
competitors.why_it_works: Official, trusted, free/low-cost; direct ties to US universities and the U.S. Embassy.
competitors.take: Partner rather than compete: co-host webinars, link to EducationUSA events, and consider the U.S. Mission's EducationUSA grant calls for joint programmes.
competitors.difference: EducationUSA covers only US study; Meridian spans all destinations, test prep, tutors and non-degree programmes in one bilingual product.

competitors.name: Qatar admissions consultancies (Quad Education, H&C Education, J&J Education, Right Track Qatar, Sahara)
competitors.what: Mix of US-based firms marketing remote counselling to Doha international-school families (Quad, H&C, J&J) and Qatar-based firms offering admissions, scholarships, profile building, test prep and visa support (Right Track, Sahara).
competitors.model: Premium B2C consulting packages; prices not published.
competitors.pricing: Not published.
competitors.scale: No verifiable scale; J&J claims 94% of applicants accepted to top choices (self-reported, unverified).
competitors.why_it_works: Qatar has a high-income expat and national population at international schools (e.g. American School of Doha, Qatar Academy) willing to pay for US/UK admissions help.
competitors.take: In Qatar, Meridian can price higher than in Georgia and target international-school families with a premium human tier.
competitors.difference: Most are remote US firms with no Qatar-specific product; Meridian's founders are Doha-based and can bundle opportunity discovery and tutors in Arabic/English later.

competitors.name: Qatar Career Development Center (QCDC, Qatar Foundation)
competitors.what: Qatar Foundation centre providing career guidance to secondary students, a Majors Guide for Qatari universities, Career Village events and counsellor training.
competitors.model: Publicly funded (Qatar Foundation); free events and resources.
competitors.pricing: Free events; current free one-to-one advising not confirmed.
competitors.scale: 7th Career Village (Sept 2026) hosted 3,240+ students from 160 schools; Career Counsellors Hub 2026 trained 200+ guidance professionals.
competitors.why_it_works: State backing and access to every school in Qatar; focuses on national workforce goals.
competitors.take: B2B2C route in Qatar: partner with QCDC/schools' counsellors rather than going direct-to-student only.
competitors.difference: QCDC is career/majors-oriented and Qatar-centric; Meridian adds global programmes, test prep and a tutor marketplace.

competitors.name: Preply
competitors.what: Global online tutoring marketplace, strongest in languages; tutors set prices, AI tools layered on top.
competitors.model: Commission marketplace: Preply keeps 100% of each new student's trial lesson, then 33% on later lessons, falling stepwise to 18% as the tutor's cumulative hours grow (33% to 28% after 20 hours ... 18% at 400+ hours). Students buy subscriptions/packages.
competitors.pricing: Tutor-set hourly prices; platform take 18-33% plus the full trial lesson.
competitors.scale: USD 150m Series D at a USD 1.2bn valuation (January 2026); 100,000+ tutors; users in 190+ countries; ~700 staff (2024).
competitors.why_it_works: Performance marketing at scale, subscription billing that locks in recurring lessons, tiered commission that rewards tutor loyalty, and the trial-lesson capture funds acquisition.
competitors.take: Subscription/package billing for lessons (reduces off-platform leakage), tiered take-rate that drops for loyal tutors, trial-lesson flow, tutor ranking by retention metrics.
competitors.difference: Meridian's 10% fee is far below Preply's 18-33% + 100% trial, a strong tutor-recruiting message in Georgia; Meridian is also exam/admissions-focused rather than language-hobby focused.

competitors.name: Superprof
competitors.what: French-founded tutor directory/marketplace in many countries for in-person and online lessons across 2,000+ subjects.
competitors.model: Primarily a student subscription ('Student Pass') to contact tutors; tutors list for free (optional premium membership). Sources conflict on any lesson commission (0% vs 10%).
competitors.pricing: Student Pass reported at roughly USD 39-49/month (varies by country); UK premium tutor membership reported at GBP 69/year.
competitors.scale: Company-reported: 30m+ students and teachers in 60+ countries (Nov 2025 CPO interview); Sept 2026 press release announcing acquisition of Tutors.com claims a network crossing 40 million. Turnover reported ~EUR 42m (2023, BusinessCoot).
competitors.why_it_works: SEO machine with local-language city/subject pages in dozens of countries; low cost to tutors grows supply fast.
competitors.take: SEO: Georgian-language subject x city landing pages (e.g. 'SAT tutor Tbilisi', 'IELTS Batumi').
competitors.difference: Superprof's student-subscription model has many negative billing reviews; Meridian's transparent per-lesson 10% fee avoids that trust problem.

competitors.name: italki
competitors.what: Language-learning marketplace with professional teachers and community tutors.
competitors.model: Commission per lesson: 21% on single lessons, 19% on 5-lesson packages, 17% on 10, 15% on 15-20 lesson packages, 0% on trial lessons, 30% on group classes (official support page).
competitors.pricing: Teacher-set prices; commission 15-30% depending on package.
competitors.scale: Official commission table on italki support; user/teacher totals not verified.
competitors.why_it_works: Package-based commission discounts nudge students to commit to multi-lesson bundles, reducing churn.
competitors.take: Lower Meridian fee on larger lesson packages (e.g. 10% single, 8% for 10-lesson packs) to encourage commitment.
competitors.difference: italki is language-only; Meridian targets SAT/IELTS/AP/admissions and Georgian school subjects.

competitors.name: Varsity Tutors (Nerdy, NYSE: NRDY)
competitors.what: US live online tutoring company selling 'Learning Memberships' to consumers plus institutional contracts with school districts; heavy AI integration.
competitors.model: Recurring memberships (subscription) rather than per-lesson marketplace; company sets prices and pays tutors.
competitors.pricing: Membership prices not public; Q4 2025 average revenue per member USD 364/month.
competitors.scale: Q4 2025 revenue USD 49.1m (+2% YoY); Learning Memberships 85% of revenue; 33.2k active members (Nerdy earnings release).
competitors.why_it_works: Subscription revenue is predictable; public-company scale. But growth is flat, showing limits of managed tutoring and pressure from AI.
competitors.take: Membership framing ('learning plan' not single lessons) and AI between-session practice.
competitors.difference: Nerdy is US-only and expensive; Meridian is a local, low-fee marketplace plus memberships at 29-79 GEL.

competitors.name: Wyzant (IXL Learning)
competitors.what: US tutoring marketplace for in-person and online lessons; acquired by IXL Learning in 2021.
competitors.model: Tutors keep 75% (25% platform fee); students also pay a 9% service fee; tutors keep 100% for students they refer themselves.
competitors.pricing: Tutor-set hourly rates (e.g. ~USD 35-60/hr typical on its Georgia (US state) page).
competitors.scale: 65,000+ tutors at the time of the IXL acquisition (Feb 2021).
competitors.why_it_works: 0% fee on tutor-referred students turns tutors into a growth channel and discourages taking students off-platform.
competitors.take: Copy the 0%-on-referred-students rule: tutors bring their existing Georgian students onto Meridian for scheduling/payments.
competitors.difference: US-focused; Meridian's 10% is much lower than 25% + 9%.

competitors.name: Classroom.ge
competitors.what: Georgian-language tutor platform listing verified tutors by subject with ratings and prices, online and in person.
competitors.model: Appears to be commission-based: the tutor page advertises '85%' of income stays with the tutor (implying ~15% platform share; inferred, not stated).
competitors.pricing: Tutors set their own rates; site shows a range of 50-200 GEL per hour.
competitors.scale: Self-reported 5,000+ students; tutor count not stated.
competitors.why_it_works: Native Georgian UX and subject pages for national-exam subjects; verified tutor profiles.
competitors.take: Benchmark: Meridian's 10% is below Classroom.ge's implied ~15%. Match its verification and Georgian subject taxonomy.
competitors.difference: Classroom.ge is tutoring-only; Meridian links tutoring to admissions goals (SAT/IELTS for a target programme) and to the opportunity database.

competitors.name: Gakvetili.ge and classifieds (gurus.ge, servisebi.ge, gancxadebebi.ge)
competitors.what: Gakvetili.ge connects students with verified tutors and trial lessons; classifieds sites carry thousands of individual tutor ads (incl. 'repetitori AI' advertising ~100 GEL/month for all subjects).
competitors.model: Gakvetili.ge model not verified; classifieds are free/paid-ad listings with no payment handling.
competitors.pricing: Individual tutor rates vary; not systematically verifiable.
competitors.scale: No verified scale figures.
competitors.why_it_works: Most Georgian tutoring is informal and found via word of mouth or classifieds; low friction, no fees.
competitors.take: Meridian must offer tutors something classifieds don't: payments, scheduling, reviews, lead flow from admissions/test-prep users.
competitors.difference: Meridian adds trust (reviews, verified credentials) and goal-linked matching.

competitors.name: Opportunity Desk
competitors.what: Global listings site for scholarships, fellowships, conferences, grants, internships, plus a mentorship programme and annual Impact Challenge.
competitors.model: Free to readers; business model not publicly stated (likely advertising/sponsored posts; unverified).
competitors.pricing: Free.
competitors.scale: Self-reported 1,000,000+ monthly views (Muck Rack); Semrush estimated ~365k-527k visits/month in Q1 2025.
competitors.why_it_works: High-volume SEO content and newsletters/social distribution to young people in emerging markets.
competitors.take: Newsletter + social distribution of deadlines; Impact Challenge-style community events.
competitors.difference: Global and unverified, English-only, blog-style listings with no personalisation; Meridian offers verified, deadline-tracked, bilingual records with eligibility for Georgian/Qatari citizens and a globe UI.

competitors.name: Opportunities Circle
competitors.what: Youth network publishing scholarships, fellowships, internships, jobs and conferences.
competitors.model: Free to readers; 'Advertise With Us' suggests ad/sponsored-post revenue.
competitors.pricing: Free.
competitors.scale: 72.1k email subscribers shown on its About page (self-reported).
competitors.why_it_works: Email list built on free, frequently updated opportunity posts.
competitors.take: An email digest ('this week's deadlines for Georgian students') is a cheap retention channel.
competitors.difference: Not localised; Meridian adds Georgian-language summaries and eligibility filtering.

competitors.name: Youth Opportunities (youthop.com)
competitors.what: Free global opportunity-discovery platform for youth (education, training, jobs) with educational resources.
competitors.model: Free to youth; provider-side 'Post an Opportunity' / 'Promote Program' services suggest paid listings (pricing not published).
competitors.pricing: Free for students; promotion pricing not published.
competitors.scale: Self-described 'largest opportunity discovery platform for youth'; claims 'millions' of users (unverified).
competitors.why_it_works: Two-sided: free for youth, programme organisers pay to promote.
competitors.take: Paid 'promoted programme' slots for organisers (clearly labelled) is a realistic early revenue line for Meridian's database.
competitors.difference: Meridian can verify listings against official pages and add deadlines/eligibility specific to Georgia/Qatar.

competitors.name: Studyportals (incl. Mastersportal, Bachelorsportal)
competitors.what: Netherlands-based search portals for degree programmes worldwide.
competitors.model: Free to students; universities pay via advertising (CPM/CPC/CPL budgets) or an enrolment-based, results-only model.
competitors.pricing: Free to students; institutional pricing not published.
competitors.scale: Company claims 40m+ visitors last year with enrolments from 238 countries/territories; third-party estimate ~EUR 45.5m revenue (2022, unverified).
competitors.why_it_works: Massive programme catalogue and SEO; monetises the institution side, keeping students free.
competitors.take: Institution-pays, student-free model for Meridian's database; enrolment/lead-based pricing for Georgian and regional universities and summer schools.
competitors.difference: Studyportals covers degrees only; Meridian covers high-school-age programmes (UWC, FLEX, summer schools, youth exchanges) plus prep and tutoring.

competitors.name: Scholarships.com
competitors.what: Free US scholarship search engine with profile matching (since 1998).
competitors.model: Free to students; ad-supported (per third-party descriptions).
competitors.pricing: Free.
competitors.scale: Third-party sources cite ~3.7m listed scholarships and grants worth ~USD 19bn (unverified).
competitors.why_it_works: Profile-matching against a very large database; long-standing SEO authority.
competitors.take: Profile-based matching (student fills profile once, gets matched programmes).
competitors.difference: US-centric awards mostly unavailable to Georgian/Qatari students; Meridian filters by citizenship eligibility.

competitors.name: Bold.org
competitors.what: US platform where donors create scholarships and students apply via one profile.
competitors.model: Donor-funded scholarships administered via the Bold Foundation (501(c)(3)); donors pay 0 fees per Bold; company monetisation details not verified.
competitors.pricing: Free for students.
competitors.scale: Bold claims 'millions of students' on the platform (self-reported); platform-wide totals not verified.
competitors.why_it_works: Makes it easy for donors to create named scholarships; students reuse one profile across many applications.
competitors.take: A 'create a scholarship' tool for Georgian diaspora, alumni and companies could seed local scholarships on Meridian.
competitors.difference: US-only eligibility; Meridian can host Georgia/Qatar-specific awards.

competitors.name: Youth Platform (youthplatform.gov.ge)
competitors.what: Georgian government youth portal organising scholarships, online courses and exchange programmes by category.
competitors.model: Publicly funded.
competitors.pricing: Free.
competitors.scale: No usage figures found.
competitors.why_it_works: Official status and Georgian language.
competitors.take: Integrate/link official listings; position Meridian as the deeper, curated layer with deadlines, prep and guidance.
competitors.difference: Government portal is a listing site; Meridian adds personalisation, globe discovery, prep and counselling.

competitors.name: Common App
competitors.what: Non-profit single application used by 1,000+ US (and some international) colleges.
competitors.model: Non-profit: member colleges pay; students use it free (colleges set their own application fees; fee waivers worth ~USD 179m in FY25).
competitors.pricing: Free to students; per-college application fees set by colleges.
competitors.scale: 2024-25: 1,498,199 first-year applicants to 1,097 members; international applicants -1% that year, and reported -10% in 2025-26.
competitors.why_it_works: Network effect: one form accepted by most selective US colleges.
competitors.take: Not a competitor but a key integration: Meridian should map its guidance and essay tools to Common App prompts and deadlines.
competitors.difference: Meridian sits upstream (discovery, prep, essays) and for non-US systems (UCAS, Erasmus, UWC).

competitors.name: ApplyBoard
competitors.what: Canadian platform connecting international students and recruitment agents with institutions in Canada, US, UK, Australia.
competitors.model: B2B2C: institutions pay commissions on enrolled students; agents use the platform to submit applications.
competitors.pricing: Free to students (commissions paid by institutions).
competitors.scale: C$375m Series D (June 2021) at C$4bn valuation; 1,200+ institutions and 4,000+ recruitment partners (2020). No newer verified figures found.
competitors.why_it_works: Aggregated agent networks for institutions; scale benefits. Exposed to visa policy shocks (Canada caps since 2024).
competitors.take: Agent-network idea: Meridian could act as a vetted channel for Georgian students to partner institutions.
competitors.difference: Meridian is student-facing and multi-programme, not an agent back-office.

competitors.name: Unibuddy
competitors.what: Embeds current-student ambassadors into university websites for chat with prospective students.
competitors.model: B2B SaaS sold to universities.
competitors.pricing: Not published.
competitors.scale: USD 20m Series B (July 2021, Highland Europe), USD 32m total; ~450 HE customers in 35 countries; 80%+ of UK institutions (2021, company-reported).
competitors.why_it_works: Prospective students trust peers more than marketing; universities pay for conversion.
competitors.take: Peer mentors: Georgian students already at UWC/FLEX/US universities as paid or volunteer 'Meridian ambassadors' (a strong local trust signal).
competitors.difference: Meridian can do this cross-institution for Georgian students, in Georgian.

competitors.name: Cialfo and BridgeU (Manifest Global)
competitors.what: SaaS used by high schools and counsellors to manage university applications; both now owned by Manifest Global (BridgeU bought from Kaplan, April 2025).
competitors.model: B2B SaaS to schools; revenue also from universities/recruitment.
competitors.pricing: Not published.
competitors.scale: Cialfo USD 40m Series B (Jan 2022), USD 57m total raised.
competitors.why_it_works: Selling to schools (counsellor workflow) gives access to all students at once.
competitors.take: A school/B2B tier: offer Georgian private schools and Doha schools a counsellor dashboard on top of Meridian's data.
competitors.difference: These tools assume a school counsellor exists; most Georgian public schools have none, so Meridian goes direct-to-student.

competitors.name: Khan Academy (Official SAT practice)
competitors.what: Non-profit free learning platform; ran Official SAT Practice with College Board from 2015.
competitors.model: Non-profit, donor/philanthropy funded; free.
competitors.pricing: Free.
competitors.scale: College Board data (2017, ~250k students): 20 hours of practice associated with 115-point average gain. Khan's SAT practice product was retired 31 Dec 2023 after the digital SAT; students are now pointed to College Board's Bluebook plus Khan's digital SAT courses.
competitors.why_it_works: Free, official, high-quality content set the price of basic SAT practice to zero.
competitors.take: Don't charge for basic practice content; curate free official resources (Bluebook, Khan) and charge for personalisation, accountability and tutors. Publish hours-vs-score-gain data.
competitors.difference: Meridian adds Georgian-language explanations, tutors and admissions context; there is also a Georgian-language Khan content effort funded by a Georgian foundation.

competitors.name: Magoosh
competitors.what: Online self-paced prep for GRE, GMAT, SAT, ACT, IELTS, TOEFL.
competitors.model: One-time flat-fee access plans.
competitors.pricing: Third-party 2026 listing: SAT Premium USD 129/12 months; IELTS USD 109 (1 month) to 129 (6 months); GRE USD 149-219 (verify on magoosh.com).
competitors.scale: No verified scale/funding figures found.
competitors.why_it_works: Low-price, high-quality video + question bank; strong SEO blog.
competitors.take: Price anchor: self-paced prep at ~USD 100-130 sets a ceiling for Meridian's prep tiers.
competitors.difference: English-only, no live tutors, no local context.

competitors.name: Kaplan
competitors.what: Legacy test-prep brand with live online classes, on-demand courses and tutoring.
competitors.model: Course fees and tutoring packages.
competitors.pricing: Third-party (PrepMaven, Sept 2026): SAT live online USD 799, Live Online Plus USD 1,099, on-demand USD 199, Unlimited Prep ~USD 1,999; tutoring ~USD 115-200/hr.
competitors.scale: No verified scale figures gathered.
competitors.why_it_works: Brand trust and score guarantees; under pressure from free official content.
competitors.take: Score-improvement guarantee could be a differentiator for a premium Meridian tier, once outcome data exists.
competitors.difference: Far too expensive for Georgian families; Meridian can deliver live group classes in Georgian at local prices.

competitors.name: British Council IELTS Ready / IELTS by IDP
competitors.what: Official IELTS owners' prep: British Council's IELTS Ready (free tier with mini mock + AI feedback; Premium free when you book the test) and IDP's free 'IELTS by IDP' app.
competitors.model: Free prep used to drive test bookings (test fee is the revenue).
competitors.pricing: Free (Premium unlocked on booking).
competitors.scale: IELTS by IDP app: 160,000+ downloads after launch (IDP news). British Council free tier includes two full mock tests.
competitors.why_it_works: Bundle prep with the test they sell; official materials are trusted.
competitors.take: Integrate official free materials; monetise speaking/writing feedback by human tutors and AI.
competitors.difference: Meridian adds tutor-led speaking practice and Georgian-language support.

competitors.name: Duolingo English Test
competitors.what: Online, at-home English test accepted by many universities.
competitors.model: Test fee; free unlimited practice tests.
competitors.pricing: USD 70 per test (2026, Wikipedia); bundles vary.
competitors.scale: Official price and free practice test confirmed by Duolingo resources.
competitors.why_it_works: Cheap, convenient, fast results; free practice lowers anxiety.

positioning: No single player combines what Meridian plans: (1) a verified, deadline-tracked opportunities database covering high-school and university-age programmes (UWC, FLEX, Erasmus+, summer schools, scholarships, youth and startup programmes) with eligibility for Georgian and Qatari citizens; (2) international test prep; (3) a low-fee tutor marketplace; (4) counselling; (5) a bilingual EN/KA AI assistant. Global players each own one slice: Crimson (premium counselling, US$100m+ revenue), Preply (tutoring, US$1.2bn valuation), Studyportals (degree discovery), CollegeVine/Kollegio (free AI counsellors), Khan/British Council/IDP (free official prep). None is localised for Georgia. Locally, Georgia has (a) traditional agencies such as LEAF (since 2008; archived pricing 450 GEL per university / 1,500 GEL for 5) and commission-driven agencies, (b) the free EducationUSA centre (US only), (c) tutor platforms Classroom.ge (implied ~15% take, 50-200 GEL/hr) and Gakvetili.ge plus classifieds, (d) a government Youth Platform listing site, and (e) national-exam prep startups. There is no Georgian-language product that ties discovery, prep, tutoring and guidance together. Defensible gaps: Georgian-language content and AI; verified local data (eligibility for Georgian/Qatari passports, Georgian national committees such as UWC and FLEX); founders who are themselves outcomes (CMU, Georgetown) and can recruit a peer-mentor network; a 10% tutor fee that undercuts Preply (18-33% + 100% of trials), Wyzant (25% + 9% student fee), italki (15-21%) and Classroom.ge (~15%); and pricing (29/79 GEL) far below agency packages. Risks: (1) free substitutes (Khan, Bluebook, IELTS Ready, CollegeVine Sage, Kollegio, ChatGPT/Claude directly) compress willingness to pay for content and generic AI; (2) small Georgian market and low purchasing power, so marketplace volume may be thin; (3) tutor disintermediation (students and tutors move off-platform after matching); (4) trust: parents prefer face-to-face agencies, and unverified success claims are common locally; (5) demand shocks: Common App international applicants fell 1% in 2024-25 and a reported 10% in 2025-26, and visa policy changes hit destination choices; (6) data freshness: a programme database is only valuable if deadlines are accurate every cycle; (7) a 10% take-rate may not cover payment processing, support and acquisition costs without memberships or institutional revenue.
lessons: Give discovery and basic prep away; charge for personalisation and humans. Khan, IELTS Ready, Studyportals, CollegeVine and Kollegio are free to students. Keep the database, deadlines and a basic AI assistant free (for SEO and word of mouth). Compass and Navigator should sell accountability, tutor time, essay review and counselling, not access to information.

Add revenue from institutions and programmes alongside student revenue. Studyportals (CPM/CPC/CPL or pay-per-enrolment), Leap (university pays only after enrolment), Youth Opportunities (promoted programmes) and Unibuddy (university SaaS) all charge the supply side. Meridian can sell clearly labelled promoted listings, verified partner pages and lead or enrolment fees to Georgian/regional universities and summer schools. Like Leap's FAQ, it should say openly who pays and keep rankings independent.

Build the tutor marketplace to stop off-platform leakage. Copy Wyzant's 0% fee on students a tutor brings in themselves, Preply's subscription/package billing, and italki's lower commission on bigger packages. Keep 10% as the headline tutor-recruiting message (versus 18-33% at Preply, 25% at Wyzant and about 15% at Classroom.ge). Add scheduling, payments, reviews and lead flow so tutors have a reason to stay.

Turn outcomes into the brand, and verify them. Crimson sells on admission results, and College Board/Khan sold on '20 hours = 115 points'. Local agencies make claims nobody can check (e.g. '94% accepted'). Meridian should track and publish verified outcomes: score gains per prep hour, programme acceptances, and scholarship money won by Georgian users. The founders' own CMU/Georgetown paths can anchor this early.

Win trust locally through partners, peers and events before paid acquisition. LEAF's fairs and EducationUSA's official status are strong local trust assets. Partner with EducationUSA Tbilisi, UWC/FLEX alumni networks, Georgian schools and (in Qatar) QCDC and international-school counsellors, B2B2C in the Cialfo/BridgeU style. Run a Unibuddy-style ambassador network of Georgians already abroad. Make Georgian-language SEO pages for each programme, test and city (Superprof's playbook).

Make the AI assistant distinctly local and trustworthy rather than generic. Free AI counsellors (CollegeVine Sage, Kollegio) are already standard, and Grammarly owns generic writing fixes. Meridian's Claude assistant should answer in Georgian, rely on Meridian's verified programme records (with citations and deadlines), give admissions-specific essay feedback without ghostwriting, and hand off to a human tutor or counsellor as the paid upgrade.
local_georgia: Counselling/agencies: LEAF, the American-Georgian Education Center (https://leaf.ge; since 2008; SAT/TOEFL/IELTS prep, college counselling, twice-yearly education fair; archived pricing 450 GEL per university or 1,500 GEL for up to 5, from http://edu.aris.ge/preview/amerikul-qartuli-ganatlebis-centri-leaf/swavla-sazrvargaret-college-counseling-is-servisi.html, date unknown). Directory-listed Tbilisi agencies include ELL (est. 2001), Your Education, GAA - Georgian Academic Abroad, International Student Educational Consulting Center and Anglo-Georgia Global Group (https://www.uniagents.com/en/consultant-visa-assistance/georgia.htm). IEC (https://iec.ge) and AdAstra (https://edu.adastra.ge) mainly recruit foreign students into Georgian universities. Public/free: EducationUSA Center for International Education, Tbilisi, the only comprehensive EducationUSA centre in Georgia (https://educationusa.state.gov/centers/center-international-education-tbilisi). The U.S. Mission runs EducationUSA AI/STEM grants of USD 25-50k (https://simpler.grants.gov/opportunity/363123). Government Youth Platform (https://youthplatform.gov.ge/ka). Universities (TSU, Ilia, GTU) also publish their own exchange/scholarship pages. Tutoring: Classroom.ge (5,000+ students self-reported, tutors keep '85%', 50-200 GEL/hr; https://classroom.ge/for-teachers), Gakvetili.ge (https://gakvetili.ge), and classifieds such as gurus.ge, servisebi.ge and gancxadebebi.ge (one ad offers 'repetitori AI' at ~100 GEL/month). National-exam prep: Tehsil.ge, Coolschool.ge, and AI startups FoxPrep and Ubralod Prep (https://thestartup.ge/georgia-startups/active-startups). Khan Academy Georgian-language content funded by the David Bezhuashvili Education Foundation (https://europeanschool.ge/en/memorandum-of-understanding-with-khan-academy/). I found no Georgian-language product that combines opportunity discovery, international test prep, tutoring and counselling.
local_qatar: Counselling: mostly US-based remote firms marketing to Doha families (Quad Education, https://www.quadeducationgroup.com/locations/qatar; H&C Education, https://www.hceducationconsulting.com/doha-college-admissions-consulting/; J&J Education, https://www.jandjeducation.com/areas/doha-college-consultants, which claims 94% top-choice acceptance, unverified), plus Qatar-based Right Track Consultants (https://righttrackqatar.com) and Sahara International (https://saharaedu.qa). None publish prices. Public: Qatar Career Development Center (Qatar Foundation) runs career guidance, a Majors Guide, and Career Village. The 7th edition (Sept 2026) drew 3,240+ students from 160 schools, and the 2026 counsellor hub drew 200+ professionals (https://qna.org.qa/en/News-Area/News/2026-9/30/qcdc-wraps-up-7th-career-village-with-more-than-3240-students-participating). Test prep: Manhattan Review Doha (IELTS 28-hr course USD 1,590; https://manhattanreview.com/doha-ielts-prep-courses) and 800 SAT Center (prices unpublished; https://800sat.org/800-sat-center-qatar-the-best-sat-preparation-in-doha/). IELTS at UDST costs QAR 1,390 (paper) (https://ielts.org/test-centres/university-of-doha-for-science-technology). Willingness to pay is much higher than in Georgia, which supports a premium Qatar tier and a B2B route through international schools and QCDC.
